sec.title: Background
sec.p: T cells cooperate with the intestinal microbiota to coordinate antimicrobial defense, but whether this crosstalk arose as an independent innovation in mammals or represents an evolutionarily conserved feature of vertebrate immunity remains unknown.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Using the teleost Nile tilapia as a model, we demonstrate that both systemic and localized infection with Edwardsiella piscicida induce enteritis, correlated with robust intestinal T cell responses. Selective T cell depletion triggered excessive expression of proinflammatory cytokines, impaired mucosal architecture, and diminished host resistance to infection, underscoring the essential role of T cells in gut immunity. Strikingly, T cell depletion also caused profound alterations in gut microbial composition, characterized by a sharp decline in beneficial taxa such as Cetobacterium and the expansion of opportunistic pathogens including Klebsiella and Acinetobacter, indicating that T cells are required to maintain microbiome homeostasis. Conversely, broad-spectrum antibiotic eradication of the microbiota provoked hyperproliferation of intestinal T cells and barrier disruption, revealing reciprocal regulation between T cells and commensals. From the gut content, we isolated a C. somerae strain SH518, whose dietary supplementation for 6–8 weeks enhanced the activation, proliferation, and effector function of intestinal T cells, preserved mucosal homeostasis during E. piscicida challenge, and even boosted systemic T cell immunity in the spleen.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that teleost T cells engage in bidirectional interactions with gut microbiota to orchestrate both antimicrobial defense and mucosal homeostasis. We therefore propose that T cell–microbiota cooperation represents an evolutionarily ancient strategy predates terrestrial adaptation, offering new insights into the coevolution of mucosal T cell immunity and microbiome.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The gut microbiota represents one of the most influential ecological partners of vertebrates, shaping host physiology and immunity through a complex and reciprocal dialogue rather than a simple symbiotic association [1]. In mammals, accumulating evidence has demonstrated that intestinal microbes regulate immunity by guiding lymphocyte development [2], inducing regulatory T cells (Tregs) [3] and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) [4], reinforcing epithelial barrier integrity, and promoting tolerance to commensals while enabling defense against pathogens [5]. Conversely, the adaptive immune system actively sculpts microbial communities [6]: secretory IgA selectively coats commensals to establish immune exclusion [4], and T cells orchestrate mucosal homeostasis by balancing Treg-mediated tolerance with effector T cell-driven pathogen clearance [3]. Notably, T cell deficiency results in more profound dysbiosis than B cell deficiency [7], underscoring T cells as central regulators of gut microbial equilibrium. This bidirectional co-evolution between microbiota and adaptive lymphocytes has provided a cornerstone for the immunological success and evolutionary radiation of jawed vertebrates.

Teleost fish, an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates possessing adaptive immunity, offer a unique window into the evolutionary origins of microbiota–immune interactions [8, 9]. While significant progress has been made in elucidating the role of fish B cells in mucosal immunity—particularly IgM- [10] and IgT-mediated [11] regulation of microbiota and barrier defense—the relationship between intestinal T cells and the microbiota remains entirely unexplored in teleosts. Whether the coordination between T cells and intestinal microbiota represents a strategy independently acquired by mammals or a gradually evolved mechanism common to all vertebrates remains largely unknown. This gap is especially striking given that teleosts possess conserved T cell subsets and effector programs while inhabiting microbial environments far more complex and challenging than those of terrestrial vertebrates [12].

The teleost intestine retains structural features shaped by aquatic living and evolutionary ancestry. Its architecture is simple, lacking Peyer’s patches or microfold cells [13], which limits the temporal window for antigen-presenting cells to sample luminal antigens. The mucus barrier consists of a single layer, in contrast to the stratified mammalian system, thereby exposing T cells more directly to microbial antigens. Moreover, teleosts host intestinal microbial loads up to three orders of magnitude greater than mammals, dominated by Proteobacteria including pathogenic genera such as Vibrio [14]. This combination of structural simplicity and immense microbial pressure raises another key evolutionary question: how do intestinal T cells maintain mucosal immune homeostasis and regulate microbial communities in the absence of organized lymphoid structures?

Here, using Nile tilapia as a model, we provide the first evidence that intestinal T cells in teleosts mount pathogen-specific responses and orchestrate local inflammatory processes. Through T cell depletion, gut microbiota disruption, and bacterial infection models, integrated with 16S rDNA sequencing, we reveal that T cells are indispensable for shaping microbial community composition and maintaining intestinal immune equilibrium. Furthermore, dietary supplementation with Cetobacterium, a T cell-regulated commensal, enhances host resistance to infection through modulating T cell activation and effector functions, highlighting a reciprocal interaction in which commensal microbes reinforce T cell responses. Together, these findings establish T cells as central architects of gut immune–microbiota homeostasis in an early vertebrate lineage. By uncovering the dual role of intestinal T cells—coordinating defense against pathogens while sustaining microbial balance—our study illuminates a conserved framework of host–microbiota interaction that predates terrestrial adaptation and highlights the evolutionary origins of T cell-mediated mucosal immunity.

sec.title: E. piscicida infection triggers T cell responses in the gut of tilapia
sec.p:
Because the distribution and function of immune cells may differ along the intestinal tract, the tilapia intestine was divided into foregut and hindgut according to anatomical characteristics in this study. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that CD3ε⁺ T cells constitute approximately 20–30% of lymphocytes in foregut and hindgut (Fig. 1A). In vitro stimulation of gut leukocytes with the T cell–specific mitogen PHA induced robust phosphorylation of key signaling molecules required for T cell activation, including NF-κB p65, JNK, ERK1/2, and S6 (Fig. S1A). Consistently, TCR engagement by anti-CD3ε plus anti-CD28 mAbs markedly enhanced ERK1/2 and S6 phosphorylation in both foregut and hindgut CD3ε⁺ T cells (Fig. S1B), confirming the capacity of intestinal T cells to respond to antigen receptor-mediated stimulation. To assess the role of gut T cells in antibacterial immunity, we established a systemic infection model via intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of E. piscicida. Infected tilapia exhibited shortened intestinal tracts (Fig. 1B, S1C), villus damage accompanied by inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 1C), and significant body weight loss (Fig. 1D). In addition, leukocytes isolated from the foregut, hindgut, spleen, or peripheral blood displayed decreased AKP/ALP activities (Fig. 1E) and increased ROS levels (essential upstream trigger for the inflammatory response in tilapia) [15] (Fig. 1F, S1D, S1E), indicating pronounced intestinal inflammation and oxidative stress. Within this inflammatory milieu, gut T cells were strongly activated upon bacterial challenge, as evidenced by elevated phosphorylation of JNK, ERK1/2, and S6 (Fig. 1G, 1H), along with increased expression of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17A, and IL-21 (Fig. 1I, S1F) in leukocytes or gated CD3ε⁺ T cells. Concordantly, both the proportion and number of CD3ε⁺ T cells in the total gut were significantly increased at 5 days post-infection (dpi) (Fig. S1G-I). Meanwhile, CD3ε⁺ T cells in foregut and hindgut expanded significantly (Fig. 1J, 1 K), driven by enhanced proliferative activity (Fig. 1L, 1M). In particular, the frequencies of CD4-1+ T cells that expressing IFN-γ (Fig. S1J, S1K) or IL-17A, representing Th1 or Th17 cells respectively, were obviously or slightly increased (Fig. S1L, S1M). E. piscicida infection also induced the apoptosis of gut T cells (Fig. 1N, 1O), suggesting a homeostatic mechanism that limits excessive T cell accumulation during infection. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that systemic E. piscicida infection not only causes enteritis but also elicits robust intestinal T cell responses in tilapia.Fig. 1

sec.title: Local infectious and chemical enteritis drive intestinal T cell responses
sec.p:
Given that systemic infection triggered both intestinal pathology and gut T cell responses, we next employed an oral gavage model of E. piscicida infection to examine whether local enteritis is sufficient to activate intestinal T cells. Oral infection induced marked intestinal pathology, including higher bacterial titer in gut than spleen (Fig. S2A), villus damage and inflammatory infiltration (Fig. 2A), gut shortening (Fig. 2B, 2 C), increased intestinal permeability (Fig. 2D), and significant body weight loss (Fig. 2E). Notably, AKP/ALP activity was significantly reduced in foregut and hindgut leukocytes, but remained unchanged in the spleen (Fig. 2F). Likewise, ROS levels were elevated in gut lymphocytes, whereas spleen and peripheral blood leukocytes displayed no detectable alterations (Fig. 2G), thereby confirming the establishment of a gut-specific infection model characterized by localized inflammation. Within this intestinal milieu, gut T cells mounted a pronounced response. Effector cytokines, including IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17A, and IL-21, were significantly upregulated in gut leukocytes (Fig. 2H, S2B), correlated with enhanced T cell activation (Fig. 2I). By 5 dpi, the proportion and absolute number of CD3ε⁺ T cells in total gut were significantly increased (Fig. S2C-E). Meanwhile, the proportion of CD3ε⁺ T cells in both foregut and hindgut had expanded markedly (Fig. 2J, 2 K), driven by active proliferation (Fig. 2L, 2M) and accompanied by increased apoptosis (Fig. 2N, 2O). In contrast, T cell frequencies in the spleen remained stable throughout infection (Fig. S2F, S2G). Similar with the results observed during systemic infection, the frequencies of Th1 and Th17 cells were significantly increased upon oral gavage infection by E. piscicida (Fig. S2H-K). These results demonstrate that local E. piscicida infection is sufficient to induce enteritis and drive compartmentalized T cell responses in the gut of tilapia.Fig. 2

To further establish the link between intestinal inflammation and gut T cell responses, a TNBS-induced chemical enteritis model was employed. By day 4 post-exposure, the foregut displayed villus tip edema and structural disruption, while the hindgut was characterized by dense inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 3A). During the acute phase (day 1), markedly increased MPO activity indicated a neutrophil-dominated response, which subsequently declined by day 4, coinciding with lymphocyte expansion (Fig. 3B, S2L, S2M). This shift was correlated with elevated expression of proinflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IFN-γ and IL-1β and chemokines MCP-1 and CXCR2 (Fig. 3C), collectively shaping a microenvironment favorable for T cell recruitment and activation. Notably, significant increases in CD3ε⁺ and CD3ε⁺CD4-1⁺ T cells were detected in the foregut, but not in the hindgut (Fig. 3D-3F), underscoring a segment-specific T cell response. However, a significant increase of myeloid cells was observed to correlate with the decrease of lymphocytes in hindgut at day 4 (Fig. 3G, H), indicating the potential contribution of myeloid cells in the hindgut inflammation in this TNBS model. This was further confirmed by elevated enzymatic activity of the MPO (neutrophils) and LZM (macrophages) in hindgut tissues (Fig. 3I, J). Together with the oral infection model, our study supports a notion that gut T cells play central roles in mounting immune responses and intestinal inflammation in teleost.Fig. 3

sec.title: T cell depletion disrupts gut integrity and impairs antibacterial immunity
sec.p:
Since intestinal T cells actively participate in gut immune responses during inflammation, we next assessed their functional importance using T cell-selective depletion strategy. Tilapia were i.p. injected with mouse anti-tilapia CD3ε mAb followed by tilapia anti-mouse IgG serum. Two weeks post-treatment, T cells in both foregut and hindgut were reduced by more than 80% compared with controls (Fig. 4A, 4B), which was further confirmed by decreased transcription of T cell marker TCRβ, CD4-1, and CD8α (Fig. 4C). Histological analysis revealed pronounced structural injury in the intestine of T cell-depleted fish, including villus tip edema and broadening, serrated epithelial lesions, inflammatory infiltration, and basement membrane thinning in the foregut, as well as villus luminal dilation in the hindgut (Fig. 4D, 4E). Consistently, leukocytes from depleted fish exhibited significantly elevated expression of proinflammatory cytokine TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-17A, and IL-21 (Fig. 4F), indicating an uncontrolled inflammatory response in the absence of gut T cells. Functionally, T cell loss severely compromised host resistance to infection. Following E. piscicida challenge, T cell-depleted tilapia displayed markedly impaired T cell expansion in both foregut and hindgut at 5 dpi (Fig. 4G, 4H), correlated with a substantial increase in bacterial burden within the intestine (Fig. 4I). Since we have reported that T cell depletion increases tilapia mortality upon E. piscicida infection [16], these results demonstrate that gut T cells are indispensable for preserving mucosal barrier integrity, restraining excessive inflammation, and orchestrating effective antibacterial defense of this early vertebrate, thereby supporting a notion that the dual role of gut T cells in barrier maintenance and antibacterial defense is evolutionarily conserved in vertebrates, already evident in teleost.Fig. 4

sec.title: T cells depletion causes gut microbiota dysbiosis
sec.p:
Given the close interplay between gut microbiota and host immune responses, we next investigated whether T cells shape intestinal immunity via controlling microbial communities. To this end, 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing was performed on foregut and hindgut contents from control and T cell-depleted tilapia. Following T cell depletion, α-diversity indices (Sob, Chao1, ACE) increased significantly in both intestinal segments (Fig. 5A), indicating enhanced microbial richness and evenness. β-diversity analysis revealed substantial restructuring of microbial communities in both foregut and hindgut (R2 > 0.25, P < 0.05), demonstrating widespread dysbiosis along the intestinal tract (Fig. 5B). In control fish, foregut and hindgut harbored distinct microbial compositions. The foregut was predominantly occupied by Fusobacteriota and Proteobacteria, whereas the hindgut exhibited higher diversity, with Fusobacteriota (41.3%), Bacteroidota (32.0%), and Proteobacteria (22.5%) co-dominating (Fig. 5C). Depletion of T cells caused dramatic shifts: the foregut experienced near-complete loss of Fusobacteriota, with blooms of Proteobacteria and Firmicutes, while the hindgut became overwhelmingly dominated by Proteobacteria, accompanied by reductions in Fusobacteriota and Bacteroidota and an increase in Firmicutes (Fig. 5C). Indicator species and heatmap analyses confirmed significant phylum-level reorganizations, particularly pronounced in the hindgut (Fig. 5D, 5E). At the genus level, T cell depletion increased microbial diversity in both foregut and hindgut segments (Fig. 5F, S3A), reflected by higher genus richness and broader taxonomic representation. LEfSe analysis (LDA score > 4.0, FDR < 0.01) identified distinct microbial signatures: in the foregut, 23 taxa including Bacilli, Burkholderiales, and Exiguobacterales were enriched, while core commensals such as Cetobacterium and other Fusobacteria lineages were depleted (Fig. 5G, S3B). In the hindgut, Proteobacteria, Acinetobacter, Moraxellaceae, Pseudomonadales, and Klebsiella became dominant, with corresponding reductions in Fusobacteria and Cetobacterium (Fig. 5H, S3C). Consistently, operational taxonomic units (OTUs) increased markedly after T cell depletion—from 46 to 563 in the foregut and from 79 to 245 in the hindgut (Fig. S3D)—indicating rapid shifts in ecological niche allocation. Notably, we demonstrated that the activated foregut T cells tilapia are capable of producing IL-22 (Fig. S3E). Given the critical role of IL-22 in maintaining intestinal barrier function and mucosal homeostasis [27, 28], we suggest that the impaired intestinal homeostasis upon T cell depletion may be associated with the loss of IL-22-producing T cells. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that gut T cells play a critical role in maintaining microbial homeostasis in tilapia, and their depletion leads to substantial dysbiosis characterized by increased diversity, loss of core commensals, and expansion of potentially pathogenic taxa.Fig. 5

sec.title: Gut dysbiosis causes spontaneous T-cell response and intestinal inflammation
sec.p:
Building on the finding that T cells shape microbial community composition, we next examined the reciprocal influence of gut microbiota on host T-cell immunity. To this end, tilapia were subjected to broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment with ampicillin (Amp) and kanamycin (Kan) by daily oral gavage for 14 consecutive days to disrupt intestinal microbial communities. Antibiotic exposure markedly reduced overall bacterial abundance (Fig. 6A), confirming effective depletion of gut microbiota. Concomitantly, pronounced mucosal damage was observed, including epithelial disorganization and inflammatory cell infiltration in both foregut and hindgut (Fig. 6B, C), indicating that microbial perturbation precipitated local inflammation. Strikingly, during antibiotic-induced dysbiosis, CD3ε⁺ T cells from the foregut and hindgut exhibited increased ROS levels (Fig. 6D), indicating pronounced intestinal inflammation and oxidative stress; and correlated with a stronger activation, as evidenced by the elevated S6 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Fig. 6E). As a result, antibiotic treatment significantly increased the proportion of CD3ε⁺ T cells in both intestinal compartments (Fig. 6F-H), enhanced the proliferative activity (Fig. 6I-K), and promoted the production of IL-2 (Fig. 6L, M) and IFN-γ (Fig. 6N, O) by T cells. These data suggest that disruption of microbial homeostasis provokes spontaneous T-cell activation and expansion, which may represent a key driver of inflammation under dysbiotic conditions. Together with the preceding findings, these results highlight a bidirectional regulatory relationship: while T cells are critical in maintaining microbial balance, gut microbes in turn exert a profound influence on T-cell activity. Such mutual regulation is essential for sustaining intestinal homeostasis and ensuring appropriate mucosal immune responses.Fig. 6

sec.title: T cell depletion perturbs gut microbiota with a marked decline in Cetobacterium
sec.p:
To delineate microbial taxa regulated by T cells, we reanalyzed 16S rDNA sequencing data from T cell-depleted tilapia. Loss of T cells provoked a profound reorganization of the gut microbiota at the genus level (Fig. 7A, 7B, Fig. S4A). Strikingly, Cetobacterium—a dominant commensal—dropped from 52.5% to 0.9% in the foregut and from 41.3% to 0.9% in the hindgut (Fig. 7A). This collapse was accompanied by the expansion of opportunistic or pathogenic genera, including Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Citrobacter, and Exiguobacterium (Fig. 7A). Quantitative analysis confirmed a drastic reduction of Cetobacterium across both gut regions (Fig. 7B). Circos plots further highlighted this microbial shift, showing that dominant taxa in control fish, such as Cetobacterium and Plesiomonas, were replaced by Exiguobacterium, Comamonas, Klebsiella, and Acinetobacter in T cell-depleted fish (Fig. 7C). Among all taxa, Cetobacterium emerged as the most distinctive biomarker separating control and T cell-depleted fish, exhibiting a consistent and pronounced loss across community-level and taxon-specific analyses (Fig. 7D-F). Together, these results identify Cetobacterium as a keystone commensal maintained by T cells, and suggest that its depletion serves as a pivotal event linking T cell loss to gut dysbiosis and heightened risk of pathogen overgrowth.Fig. 7

sec.title: Cetobacterium primes intestinal T cell activation and effector function in tilapia
sec.p:
To further assess the immunomodulatory potential of Cetobacterium, we isolated a Cetobacterium somerae strain (designated SH518, NCBI GenBank Accession No. PX285878) from the intestinal contents of Nile tilapia (Fig. 8A). To determine its effects on the immunity, tilapia were fed with SH518-supplemented diets for 6–8 weeks (Fig. 8B). SH518 supplementation had no significant impact on the frequency of CD3ε⁺ T cells in gut (Fig. 8C, 8D), although a slight increase in body weight was noted (Fig. S4B). Strikingly, in SH518-fed fish, CD3ε⁺ T cells from the foregut displayed markedly enhanced phosphorylation of S6 and ERK1/2 upon CD3ε/CD28 stimulation (Fig. 8E, S4C, S4D), indicating a robust activation; whereas S6 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation were only slightly enhanced in the hindgut T cells (Fig. 8E, S4C, S4D). Moreover, following P + I stimulation, these T cells produced substantially greater amounts of IL-2 (Fig. 8F, 8G) and IFN-γ (Fig. 8H, 8I). sec.title: Cetobacterium supplementation enhances T cell–mediated protection against intestinal and systemic infection
sec.p:
To further assess whether Cetobacterium-modulated intestinal T cell response confers resistance to infection, tilapia were challenged with E. piscicida after 6–8 weeks of dietary supplementation with strain SH518. Compared with fish receiving the control diet, SH518-fed tilapia displayed significantly higher proportions of T cells in both the foregut and hindgut (Fig. 9A, B), driven by enhanced activation capacity (Fig. 9C). Intestinal T cells from these fish also produced markedly greater amounts of IL-2 (Fig. 9D, E) and IFN-γ (Fig. 9F, G). These improvements translated into more efficient clearance of intestinal E. piscicida (Fig. 9H). Importantly, the protective effects of SH518 supplementation extended beyond the intestine. During systemic infection by i.p. injection with E. piscicida, T cells from SH518-fed tilapia exhibited stronger activation response (Fig. 9I), showed increased T cell abundance (Fig. 9J, K) and proliferation (Fig. 9L, S4E), as well as elevated IL-2 (Fig. 9M, N) and IFN-γ (Fig. 9O, P) production in the spleen, thereby enhancing the ability of tilapia to clear the E. piscicida infection (Fig. 9Q). Together, these findings demonstrate that Cetobacterium supplementation potentiates both local and systemic T cell immunity, thus strengthening host defense against bacterial challenge in early vertebrates.Fig. 9

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: T cells are pivotal executors of intestinal immunity, functioning both as effectors in pathogen elimination and as regulators of mucosal homeostasis in mammals [17, 18]. Our findings demonstrate that this dual functionality is also preserved in teleost fish such as tilapia, despite the absence of organized mucosal lymphoid structures like Peyer’s patches. We observed abundant intestinal T cells actively engaged in immune responses, and through E. piscicida infection and TNBS-induced enteritis models, we established that these cells operate not only as direct antimicrobial effectors but also as modulators restraining excessive inflammation. This mirrors the antigen-specific responses mediated by CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells in mammals [17, 19], underscoring a striking evolutionary conservation. Notably, selective depletion of T cells aggravated inflammatory response. Effector T-cell subsets such as Th1 and Th17 cells are indeed major producers of pro-inflammatory cytokines [20, 21]. In our study, the depletion strategy targeted total T-cell population in tilapia, without distinguishing among functional sub-lineages. We therefore speculate that the exacerbated inflammation observed after T-cell depletion is likely attributable to the loss of Treg cells. This interpretation is consistent with extensive evidence from mammalian systems. In mice, Tregs represent a specialized CD4⁺ T-cell lineage indispensable for maintaining gut immune tolerance and homeostasis; and selective elimination of Tregs is sufficient to trigger severe and even lethal colitis [22, 23]. Thus, it is plausible that a similar imbalance—caused by the depletion of tilapia Tregs—underlies the uncontrolled inflammatory response we observed. However, due to the lack of antibodies for tilapia CD25 and Foxp3, we still cannot figure out the detail contribution of Treg cells in this fish species. Selective depletion of T cells also disrupted intestinal architecture, and impaired antibacterial defense, confirming their indispensable role in maintaining barrier integrity. Collectively, these findings indicate that intestinal T cells represent an ancient and conserved immune strategy, acting as central orchestrators of both antimicrobial defense and tissue homeostasis. Despite architectural divergence in mucosal immune systems, the essential functions of intestinal T cells appear to have been established early in vertebrate evolution and maintained across species, offering compelling evidence for the evolutionary continuity of mucosal immunity and the enduring significance of T cells in host adaptation.

Teleost fish occupy a pivotal evolutionary position in the transition of jawed vertebrates from aquatic to terrestrial environments [24, 25], making them an ideal model for exploring ancestral modes of intestinal immune regulation. Using Nile tilapia, we investigated the interplay between intestinal T cells and the microbiota. T-cell depletion not only impaired pathogen clearance but also induced a distinct pattern of dysbiosis, characterized by abnormally elevated α-diversity and profound structural collapse of the microbial community. This response stands in sharp contrast to mammals, where T-cell deficiency typically associates with reduced α-diversity and TNF-α–driven inflammatory pathology [26]. This fundamental difference raises a profound question: does it reflect a more foundational role for T cells in maintaining barrier integrity within a “primitive” immune system that lacks sophisticated structures like Peyer’s patches? Our data confirmed this notion. We speculate that this divergence reflects severe epithelial barrier disruption in fish following T-cell loss. In tilapia that lacking Peyer’s patches, intestinal T cells are diffusely distributed. Upon T cell depletion, the gut’s physical barrier collapses, allowing massive influx of pathogens and exogenous antigens, which in turn drives catastrophic microbiota perturbation. Furthermore, not only were there significant differences in intestinal microbiota diversity between gut regions in tilapia, but intestinal immune responses also displayed marked regional specialization. In both systemic and oral infection models, the hindgut mounted stronger T-cell responses, consistent with its enrichment of T cells, underscoring the central role of T cells in maintaining hindgut microbial stability. In addition, mammalian T cells help preserve epithelial integrity by producing cytokines such as IL-22, which promote barrier function and mucus secretion [27, 28]. Similarly, in the present study, we demonstrate that intestinal T cells in tilapia are capable of secreting IL-22. This finding aligns with our previous study that activated spleen T cells in tilapia can produce IL-22 [29], further suggesting the potential role of tilapia T cells in regulating epithelial integrity via producing IL-22. Beyond T cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) can also produce IL-22. Studies using single-cell RNA sequencing have identified ILC-like populations in teleost [30, 31], suggesting ILC-like cells may be another contribution for producing IL-22 and maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and homeostasis in tilapia. In TNBS-induced enteritis, the foregut exhibited pronounced T-cell activation, indicating that foregut T cells, although typically quiescent, retain the capacity for robust responses under pathological conditions. This inducible activation likely reflects an evolutionary adaptation: as the primary entry point for food and pathogens [32], the foregut requires T cells with a “conditional” rather than “constitutive” activation mode, enabling efficient pathogen clearance while minimizing the metabolic cost of continuous activation. Such functional plasticity highlights a refined eco-immunological balance shaped during vertebrate evolution.

The regionalized and diffusely organized intestinal immune strategy observed in tilapia stands in sharp contrast to the mammalian paradigm, which relies on Peyer’s patches to concentrate antigen sampling and orchestrate follicular responses [33]. From this comparison, we propose a stepwise evolutionary model of intestinal immunity in jawed vertebrates. In early vertebrates such as teleost fish, diffuse lymphocyte distribution coupled with regionally specialized immune microenvironments provided a primitive yet effective framework for infection defense. Correspondingly, the structure of its gut microbiota is relatively simple, yet core taxa such as the genus Cetobacterium play a critical role in coordinating immune and metabolic functions [34, 35]. Amphibians represent the next stage, with intestines already showing nascent lymphoid aggregates, such as identifiable lymphoid follicles in frogs [36], indicating a transitional state from diffuse to organized structures. Birds and mammals then evolved highly developed secondary lymphoid structures, exemplified by Peyer’s patches [37], which enable efficient antigen surveillance and optimized adaptive immune responses [38]. Importantly, the microbiota-immune interaction network also exhibited increased complexity in mammals [39, 40]. For example, colonization of germ-free mice with the specific commensal bacterium segmented filamentous bacteria induces the activation of CD4+ T cells and the production of IgA [41]; while segmented filamentous bacteria can specifically induce Th17 cell differentiation, thereby finely modulating mucosal homeostasis and enhancing antimicrobial defense [39]. In contrast, Bacteroides fragilis can suppress intestinal inflammation through polysaccharide A-mediated activation of the TLR2/IL-10 pathway [42, 43]. Despite this structural progression, the central role of T cells in microbiota regulation looks remarkably conserved. Because in both mice and tilapia, T-cell deficiency results in barrier disruption and microbial dysbiosis [44], including the loss of beneficial commensals such as Clostridium spp. and expansion of Enterobacteriaceae [45]. Moreover, the cooperative function of T and B cells consistently forms the cornerstone of mucosal immunity across vertebrate lineages [46]. At the immunoglobulin level, phylogenetic analyses reveal strong homology between the constant regions of teleost IgM and mammalian IgM, highlighting its early evolutionary establishment and conservation [10]. In contrast, the functional convergence of teleost IgT and mammalian IgA in mucosal defense exemplifies independent innovation under similar ecological pressures [47]. Thus, this stepwise model not only illustrates the gradual structural sophistication of intestinal immunity but also underscores how distinct vertebrate lineages achieve functional convergence in response to shared ecological challenges.

The bidirectional interplay between intestinal microbiota and T cells represents a central axis of mucosal immune regulation [48, 49], yet its evolutionary origins remain poorly understood. Teleost fish, as early jawed vertebrates possessing primitive T cells, provide a critical model to dissect the emergence of microbe–T cell interactions. Our study reveals a reciprocal regulatory relationship between tilapia T cells and gut microbiota: disruption of microbial homeostasis triggers spontaneous T cell activation and proliferation, whereas T cell depletion induces microbial dysbiosis and expansion of opportunistic pathogens. Notably, T cell deficiency markedly reduces the abundance of Cetobacterium, a dominant native gut commensal in freshwater fish, but is rare in mammals, contributing to diverse host benefits including carbohydrate metabolism [50], vitamin B12 synthesis [51], antiviral defense [52], and ammonia detoxification [53]. Feeding experiments further demonstrate that dietary supplementation with C. somerae SH518 enhances intestinal T cell activation, proliferation, and IL-2 and IFN-γ production, thereby reinforcing anti-infective immunity. Importantly, this immunomodulatory effect extends beyond the gut to peripheral organs such as the spleen, revealing systemic immune regulatory potential. These findings strongly suggest that T cells, from their earliest evolutionary emergence, actively collaborated with gut microbes to orchestrate host immunity, exhibiting remarkable plasticity and environmental adaptability. We propose that the bidirectional T cell–microbiota interaction is not an innovation unique to mammals but represents an ancient immune cooperation common to vertebrates. Compared with terrestrial probiotics, the interaction between aquatic-derived Cetobacterium and teleost T cells demonstrates a distinct mode of host–microbe crosstalk, reflecting habitat-specific evolution of intestinal immune symbiosis. Based on these insights, we advance the “aquatic–terrestrial probiotic co-evolution” hypothesis, which provides a novel perspective on the evolutionary shaping of microbiota–immune interactions and informs the rational development of novel probiotics for aquaculture.

Given that previous studies revealed that Cetobacterium can produce some metabolites like vitamin B12 and short-chain fatty acids [51, 54–56], which are known to regulate T cell activation and function [57–59], we therefore speculate that C. somerae may promote T cell immunity in tilapia via the metabolites. However, further study is still needed to elucidate the exact mechanism by which Cetobacterium regulates T cell function in fish.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p:
Our study uncovers the conserved and indispensable roles of intestinal T cells in teleost fish, highlighting their dual function in pathogen defense and mucosal homeostasis, and their bidirectional partnership with commensal microbes, especially Cetobacterium (Fig. 10). These findings bridge fundamental gaps in our understanding of vertebrate immune evolution, revealing that core principles of T cell–microbiota crosstalk were established early and shaped by ecological pressures across habitats. Beyond evolutionary insight, the discovery of Cetobacterium–T cell cooperation provides a promising avenue for probiotic innovation in aquaculture, illustrating how ancient immune strategies can be harnessed for modern applications.Fig. 10

sec.title: Experimental animals
sec.p: Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) were obtained from an aquaculture farm located in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China. Prior to experiment, fish were maintained in a recirculating aquaculture system under controlled conditions. Water temperature was held constant at 28 °C, and aerated freshwater was provided. Fish were fed with commercial pellet twice a day. Tilapia with body length of 8–10 cm were randomly selected for experiments. This study was conducted in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals released by the Ministry of Science and Technology of China. All experiments were approved by the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of East China Normal University.

sec.title: Bacterial infection
sec.p: The Edwardsiella piscicida strain EIB202 from East China University of Science and Technology was cultured in tryptone yeast extract broth (TYB). Bacteria were harvested by centrifugation (4,000 × g, 5 min, 4 °C), washed twice with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and resuspended in PBS. The final bacterial concentration was adjusted to 2 × 107 CFU/mL for experimental infections. Systemic infection was induced by intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of 200 μL bacterial suspension, while localized intestinal infection was achieved via oral gavage of 100 μL suspension using a gavage needle carefully advanced through the esophagus. Control animals received an equivalent volume of sterile PBS administered via the corresponding routes.

sec.title: Leukocyte isolation
sec.p: Leukocytes were isolated from tilapia foregut (defined as the anterior third of the intestinal tract), hindgut (posterior third of the intestinal tract), spleen, and peripheral blood. Following removal of intestinal contents and adjacent adipose tissue, foregut and hindgut segments were treated in PBS-DTT solution (0.37 mg/mL EDTA, 0.14 mg/mL dithiothreitol) for 30 min at room temperature with constant agitation. Intestinal and spleen tissues were smashed into single-cell suspensions using Leibovitz L-15 medium (Catalog#41,300,039, Gibco), followed by filtration through nylon mesh. Peripheral blood collected via caudal venipuncture with citrate-based anticoagulant (15 mM sodium citrate, 450 mM NaCl, 0.1 M glucose, 10 mM EDTA, pH 7.0) was centrifuged and resuspended in L-15 medium. Cell suspensions were subjected to density gradient centrifugation on 52%/34% Percoll (Catalog#10,246,712, GE Healthcare) at 500 × g for 30 min with minimal acceleration/deceleration. The leukocyte-enriched fraction at the 52%−34% interface was collected, washed, and maintained in L-15 medium supplemented with 2% FBS for subsequent analyses.

sec.title: Cell stimulation
sec.p: For T cell activation, leukocytes isolated from the foregut and hindgut of Nile tilapia were cultured in DMEM medium (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin, Gibco) at 28 °C with 5% CO2, and stimulated with mouse anti-tilapia CD3ε mAb (2 μg/mL) plus anti-CD28 mAb (2 μg/mL) [16] for 6 h or with 2 μg/mL PHA (Catalog #L4144, Sigma) for 2 or 6 h. For cytokine production, leukocytes from the same tissues were additionally stimulated with PMA plus ionomycin (P + I, 50 ng/mL PMA + 500 ng/mL ionomycin) for 4 h followed by intracellular staining for IFN-γ [60] and IL-2 [61] expression in CD3ε⁺ T cells. For intracellular staining, leukocytes were activated with plate-bound anti-CD3ε mAb (2 μg/mL) plus soluble anti-CD28 mAb (2 μg/mL) for 6 h and then subjected to intracellular staining for phosphorylated S6 (p-S6, Ser240/244) (Catalog#935,703, Biolegend, 1:200) and phosphorylated ERK1/2 (p-ERK1/2, Thr202/Thy204) (Catalog#369,521, Biolegend, 1:200) in CD3ε⁺ T cells.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: 1 × 106 leukocytes from foregut and hindgut of Nile tilapia were resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS with 2%FBS). To identify CD3ε⁺ and CD4-1⁺ T cell populations, the cells were stained with biotin-conjugated mouse anti-tilapia CD4-1 mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400) [60], followed by APC-streptavidin (Catalog#405,207, BioLegend, 1:400) and FITC-conjugated anti-tilapia CD3ε mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400). For detection of CD3ε, cells were incubated with FITC-conjugated anti-tilapia CD3ε mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400) [16]. Each staining was incubated on ice for 30 min, and the cells were washed twice with FACS buffer after each staining. For apoptosis assessment, cells were stained with APC-conjugated Annexin V (Catalog#640,920, BioLegend, 1:400) in binding buffer for 15 min at room temperature. For detection of Th1 or Th17 cells, cells were incubated with biotin-conjugated anti-tilapia CD4-1 mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400), followed by APC-streptavidin and FITC-conjugated anti-tilapia IFN-γ mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400) or FITC-conjugated anti-tilapia IL-17A polyclonal antibody (1 μg/mL, 1:400) [62]. Intracellular ROS levels were detected using dihydroethidium (DHE; 5 mM) at 37 °C for 40 min in the dark, according to the manufacturer's instructions (Catalog#CA1410, Solarbio). After staining, cells were resuspended in 200 μL FACS buffer. Data acquisition was performed on a BD LSRFortessa flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software.

sec.title: BrdU incorporation
sec.p: Nile tilapia were i.p. injected with 0.75 mg/kg BrdU (Catalog#19–160, Sigma) in 200 μL PBS 16 h before the experiment, and intestinal leukocytes were isolated for the assay. The cells were incubated with FITC-labeled anti-CD3ε mAb (1 μg/mL, 1:400) on ice for 30 min, followed by fixation with BD Cytofix/Cytoperm buffer on ice for 30 min. Permeabilization was performed using BD Cytoperm Plus solution for 10 min. Then the cells were refixed with BD Cytofix/Cytoperm buffer at room temperature for 5 min and digested with 300 mg/mL DNase at 37 °C for 1 h. Samples were then stained with APC-anti-BrdU (Catalog#51-33284X, BD Biosciences, 1:400) at room temperature for 20 min. The cells were washed twice with BD Perm/Wash solution after each step. The cells were resuspended in BD Perm/Wash solution, filtered, and then analyzed with flow cytometer.

sec.title: Western blot assay
sec.p: The leukocytes of foregut and hindgut from tilapia were lysed in NP-40 lysis buffer containing phosphatase and protease inhibitors on ice for 30 min. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g, 4 °C for 10 min to obtain the supernatant protein, which was then boiled with 5 × protein loading buffer for 10 min. Proteins were separated by 12% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. The membranes were blocked with 4% skim milk in PBS with 0.05% Tween 20 (PBST) at room temperature for 1 h, and then incubated with 1:1000 diluted primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. The primary antibodies including p-NF-κB p65 (Ser536, Catalog#AF5881, Beyotime), p-Erk1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204, Catalog#4370, Cell Signaling Technology), p-JNK (Thr183/Thr183/Thr221, Catalog#AF1762, Beyotime), p-S6 (Ser240/244, Catalog#5364, Cell Signaling Technology), and mouse anti-tilapia IL-22 polyclonal antibody [29]. For the internal reference, 1:1000 diluted anti β-actin antibody (Catalog#4970, Cell Signaling Technology) was used. The blots were further incubated with goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L Alexa Fluor 800 (Catalog#5151, Cell Signaling Technology, 1:30,000) or goat anti-mouse IgG H&L Alexa Fluor 680 (Catalog#ab175775, Abcam, 1:10,000) at room temperature for 1 h. The membranes were washed with PBST for three times after each incubation and scanned finally using the Odyssey CLx Image Studio.

sec.title: Quantitative real-time RT-PCR (qPCR)
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from the leukocytes of foregut and hindgut using TRIzol reagent (Catalog#15,596,018, Invitrogen) following the manufacturer's protocol. RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using the Plus All-in-One 1 st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (Catalog#E096-1B, Novoprotein). Relative mRNA levels of target genes were quantified using NovoStart SYBR qPCR SuperMix-Plus (Novoprotein). Gene expression was normalized with β-actin, and data were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCT method. The Primers used in this study are listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Histological studies
sec.p: The foregut and hindgut tissues of tilapia were harvested and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde Fix Solution (Catalog#P0099, Beyotime) for 24 h. The samples were dehydrated in a graded ethanol solutions, cleared with xylene, and then embedded in paraffin. Tissue sections were prepared and stained following standard hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining procedures. Stained sections were observed using an Olympus BX53 light microscope, and the images were captured and analyzed with AxioVision software.

sec.title: Intestinal permeability
sec.p: On day 5 post-gavage infection, tilapia were gavaged with 100 μL of FITC solution (0.04 g/kg) dissolved in PBS. Blood samples were collected 4 h later and allowed to stand at room temperature for 2 h. The samples were then centrifuged to separate the serum, which was transferred to a black opaque 96-well plate. Fluorescence intensity in the serum was measured using a fluorescence microplate reader with an excitation wavelength of 495 nm and an emission wavelength of 520 nm. The differences in serum fluorescence intensity between the experimental and control groups were compared.

sec.title: Enzyme activity assays
sec.p: Following the manufacturer's instructions for the Myeloperoxidase (MPO) Activity Assay Kit (Catalog#BC5715, Solarbio), isolated serum or tissues were sonicated on ice and centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent analysis. The reaction mixture was prepared according to the kit protocol, thoroughly mixed, and incubated at 60 °C for 10 min. Absorbance was measured at 460 nm using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer after transferring 300 μL of the mixture to a 96-well plate. MPO enzyme activity was calculated using the liquid volume- or protein concentration- based formula provided in the kit instructions. For alkaline phosphatase (AKP/ALP) activity assessment, leukocytes were isolated from the foregut, hindgut, spleen, and peripheral blood were homogenized in 1 mL extraction buffer and centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred to a 96-well plate. According to the AKP/ALP Activity Assay Kit (Catalog#BC2140, Solarbio), samples were incubated with 5 μL ALP reaction liquid at 37 °C for 15 min. The reaction was terminated with 100 μL termination liquid, and absorbance was measured at 510 nm using an enzyme marker. AKP/ALP activity was calculated using the protein concentration-based formula provided in the instructions. Lysozyme (LZM) activity was measured using a commercial assay kit (Catalog#HB547-QT, Shanghai Hengyuan Biological) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, tissue homogenates were centrifuged, and the supernatants were incubated with the kit substrate. The change in absorbance at 450 nm was recorded, and enzyme activity was calculated based on a standard curve and normalized to total protein concentration.

sec.title: Tilapia T cell depletion
sec.p: T cell depletion was performed according to our previous report [16]. Briefly, Nile tilapia individuals were i.p. injected with 20 μg of mouse anti-tilapia CD3ε mAb, while the control group received mouse IgG1 (Catalog#401,402, BioLegend). After 24 h, the tilapia was injected with 50 μL of tilapia anti-mouse IgG1 serum and the control group received negative serum. The CD3ε antibody was supplemented twice during this period. On day 14 post-injection, intestinal leukocytes of tilapia were isolated, and the proportion of CD3ε+ T cells in the foregut and hindgut was analyzed by flow cytometry to detect the T cell depletion. Then, the T cell-depleted tilapia was i.p. injected with E. piscicida, and leukocytes from the foregut and hindgut were isolated on indicated days for subsequent experiments.

sec.title: Intestinal microbial sequencing analysis
sec.p: Total DNA was extracted from the contents using a Microbial DNA Extraction Kit. DNA concentration was quantified using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, USA), and purity was verified by 1% agarose electrophoresis. Following DNA extraction, the V3–V4 region of the 16S rDNA was amplified with barcode-specific primers 341 F (5′-CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTATCTAAT-3′). The purified amplicons were ligated with sequencing adapters to construct libraries, and paired-end sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform (Gene Denovo Biotechnology). After sequencing, raw reads were processed through quality control, denoising, merging, and chimera removal using QIIME2 and USEARCH. The similarity threshold for OTU clustering was 97%. Alpha diversity was assessed using Simpson’s diversity index (Sob), Chao1 index, and Abundance-based Coverage Estimator (ACE). Beta diversity was evaluated based on Bray–Curtis distances. Taxonomic composition of the intestinal microbiota was analyzed at the phylum and genus levels. Differences in species abundance between groups were examined using Student’s t-test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons (FDR < 0.05). A detailed bioinformatics analysis report was completed on Gene Denovo Biotechnology platform.

sec.title: Isolation and identification of Cetobacterium
sec.p: Under sterile conditions, contents from the foregut of tilapia were collected in a 1.5 mL sterile centrifuge tube, and an appropriate volume of sterile PBS was added to create a homogenate. A 0.1 mL aliquot of the homogenate was transferred to a new tube containing 0.9 mL sterile PBS to prepare a 10–1 dilution. Successive dilutions of 10–2, 10–3, 10–4, 10–5, and 10–6 were prepared similarly. 100 μL of each dilution were spread on Gifu Anaerobic Medium (GAM) solid anaerobic medium (Catalog#HB8518-1, Haibo Biology). The inoculated plates were placed in an anaerobic culture bag and incubated at 28 °C for 24–48 h. Colonies with appropriate density and different morphologies were picked and cultured in GAM liquid anaerobic medium at 28 °C for 24 to 48 h. DNA was extracted from the cultured bacteria and amplified using universal bacterial primers 27 F and 1492R. The amplified products were sequenced by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai). The sequences were compared with the NCBI database to identify the species of the isolated bacteria.

sec.title: Phylogenic analysis
sec.p: To validate the Cetobacterium identification, genomic sequences of additional Cetobacterium strains were retrieved from GenBank. Multiple sequence alignment was performed using ClustalX, and a phylogenetic tree was constructed in MEGA7 using the neighbor-joining (NJ) method with 1000 bootstrap replications. The evolutionary relationships among these strains were comparatively analyzed based on the phylogenetic tree. Accession numbers for all sequences used in this analysis are provided in Table S2.

sec.title: Cetobacterium feeding experiment
sec.p: The tilapia (1–2 g) were acclimatized for two weeks in an aquaculture system under standard commercial feeding. After acclimatization, the fish were randomly divided into two groups, with each group comprising three 30-L glass tanks (30 fish/tank). The control group were fed the standard commercial diet, while the treatment group received the same commercial diet supplemented with Cetobacterium somerae at 107 CFU/g. The feeding rate was maintained at 3% of body weight, with two feedings per day. A 50% daily water exchange was performed throughout the trial. Subsequent experiments were conducted between 6–8 weeks of the feeding trial.

sec.title: Antibiotic administration
sec.p: A 100 μL mixture of antibiotics (ampicillin, 25 mg/mL; kanamycin, 25 mg/mL) was gavaged to Nile tilapia, while being maintained in antibiotic-supplemented water. Control groups received an equal volume of PBS. The tilapia were fasted for 24 h before the experiment. Water was changed and antibiotics replenished every 72 h. After 14 days of antibiotic treatment, the intestines were collected. Samples from the foregut and hindgut were processed for fixation and leukocyte isolation as described above. The contents of the midgut were inoculated onto LB agar plates and cultured overnight at 37 °C. The effect of antibiotics on the intestinal microbiota was assessed by colony counting.

sec.title: Induction of colitis with TNBS
sec.p: An ethanol solution of 2,4,6-Trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS, Catalog #p2297, Sigma) was prepared by mixing a 5% (W/V) TNBS aqueous solution with anhydrous ethanol in a 2:1 volume ratio, resulting in a final concentration of 2.5%, and used immediately after preparation. The tilapia were fasted for 24 h before the experiment. One day later, the experimental group was gavaged with 100 µL 2.5% TNBS ethanol solution, while the control group received an equal volume of saline. Afterwards, normal feeding was resumed. The intestinal samples were collected on indicated days for subsequent analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The results are expressed as mean ± SEM, and statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed Student’s t-test. P-values are categorized as follows: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001.
